title: Imitation (I.1)
hookLine: anyone can copy a star's haircut; the Imitation of Christ opens on following, not copying
tomorrow: can you know exactly what sorry means and never feel it?
last: GIVE WHAT YOU ASK · IF NO ONE ASKS · IN CHARITY.

cards: Anybody can copy a star's haircut, or the song they walk out to. That's copying. Following is something else: taking on how they train, what they care about, where they go when nobody's filming.
The Imitation of Christ opens on that difference. Its first line is from the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness."

teach.b: Then the book explains itself. These are the words of Christ, it says, telling us to imitate his life and his ways if we want to be truly enlightened and free of blindness of heart.
So the first thing to study, it says, is the life of Jesus. Not a costume, not a pose. A life to learn by heart until it shapes yours.
That's the word today, and it's lighter than it sounds.
Imitation in this book doesn't mean a copy. It means following, step after step, the way a child learns a family's way of laughing without a manual.
And notice how this week's lines lead into it. Augustine asked God for the strength to do what God asks. He admitted some things you know only by living them.
He argued in charity, rested in God, owned up and praised.
A book for beginners now names the beginning: follow.

how: Catholics read the Gospels and pray over scenes from Jesus's life, as in the rosary's mysteries, so his life can shape theirs; The Imitation of Christ is one classic guide for that.

o: following a life until it shapes your own

games.q: a younger teammate starts wearing your cleats, your hairstyle, your warm-up song. what would imitation in the book's sense look like instead?
o: learning how you treat people and why you train, not your look.
an even closer copy of your cleats, your hair and your song.
never looking up to anyone, so she stays fully original.
games.why: the Imitation's following is about a life and its ways, not its surface: make his life your first study, and let it shape yours.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing Jesus does in the Gospels: noticing someone overlooked, sharing a meal, speaking kindly to a stranger.
Then picture one person you'll see tomorrow, and choose the one small act you could follow him in, and let the choice settle.

wordCard.voice: Imitation. In this book, not copying a look but following a life: the life of Jesus, studied until it shapes yours.
